911.title: Richard Allen (1794)
911.hook: pulled from his knees in a segregated church, he founds the African Methodist Episcopal Church
911.howItsDone: The African Methodist Episcopal Church remembers Richard Allen as its founder, and Mother Bethel in Philadelphia still gathers for worship on the same ground.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Korea's lay founders, who read of cheonju and began a church before any priest arrived. Your line was the laity began it. Who did you share your one sentence with? Day nine hundred eleven.

Sunday morning in Philadelphia. The prayer has already begun, and a group of Black Methodists are on their knees in the gallery of a church they had given money to finish. Then a hand grabs one of them, a man named Absalom Jones, and tries to haul him to his feet. A church officer is telling him he's kneeling in the wrong place. Jones asks to be allowed to finish praying first. The officer won't wait. Kneeling nearby, a preacher who had once been enslaved sees all of it. Today: Richard Allen.

We have this story in Allen's own words. He wrote an account of his life, and it's plain and unshowy. He was born enslaved, came to faith among the Methodists, and, his account says, the man who held him in slavery heard a Methodist preacher, came to believe slavery was wrong, and agreed to let Allen buy his freedom. Allen worked, paid, and was free. He preached in Philadelphia, and Black worshipers came to hear him in growing numbers. Then came that Sunday. They were told to sit in the gallery, and when they knelt in what they thought was the right place, an officer pulled Jones up off his knees in the middle of the prayer. When the prayer ended, Allen writes, "we all went out of the church in a body". They didn't stay to argue. They didn't burn anything down. They walked out together. And then they built. Allen's account tells of buying an old blacksmith's shop, hauling it onto a lot, and fitting it out as a place to worship. It was called Bethel, the house of God. Out of it grew the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and Allen became its bishop. Paul wrote to the Galatians: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." Allen's church did not walk away from Methodism or from that verse. It walked away from a gallery, and built a house where nobody would be pulled off their knees.
screen: `PULLED UP IN THE MIDDLE OF PRAYER.`
`WE ALL WENT OUT IN A BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand with someone who was pushed out. Close your eyes if that's comfortable. Bring to mind someone who has been left out lately. At work, at school, in a family, in a group chat, in a church. Picture where they are standing, a little outside the circle. Then picture yourself walking over and standing next to them. Not fixing anything yet. Just standing there. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just keep them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Richard Allen. A preacher born enslaved who bought his freedom, walked out of a segregated church with his people, and helped found the African Methodist Episcopal Church.
Your line: we all went out. Today, take one real step toward the person you pictured. Sit with them, message them, include them, so they aren't standing alone. Day nine hundred eleven.

912.title: Olaudah Equiano
912.hook: kidnapped as a child, he buys his freedom, writes his story, and fights the slave trade
912.howItsDone: Equiano's narrative is read in schools and churches, and many readers remember him alongside others who worked against the slave trade.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Richard Allen, walking out of a church with his people and building Bethel. Your line was we all went out. Who did you stand next to? Day nine hundred twelve.

"Written by Himself." Three words on the title page of a book, and they are doing a lot of work. The man who wrote them had been sold as a child, carried across the ocean in a slave ship, and given a new name by the men who owned him. He put it right on the title page: this is my story, and I wrote it. He sold the book himself, from town to town, and spoke wherever people would listen. Today: Olaudah Equiano.

His book is called The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African. Both names are in the title on purpose. Olaudah Equiano is the name he says he was born with, in an Igbo village in West Africa. Gustavus Vassa is the name an owner gave him. In the book he tells of being kidnapped with his sister, of being torn apart from her, and of the slave ship: the crowding, the stench, the people who chose to jump into the sea rather than go on. He was sold more than once. Under a Quaker merchant in the Caribbean, he traded a little on the side, saved every coin, and bought his freedom. Then he came to a deep Christian faith, and the book tells that story too, full of scripture. And here is what he did with all of it. He told it. He used scripture, the book his British readers knew, to show them what the trade was doing. A psalm says: "Let the redeemed of the LORD say so." Say so: tell it out loud. Equiano did, plainly, as the one who had lived it, and his readers could not unhear it. Some historians have asked whether he was born in Africa, or gathered his memories of it from others. Others defend his account. Either way, his voice on the page is what readers met, and the movement against the trade used it.

Here's the practice: honor an enslaved person's account by listening for it. Breathe out slowly, twice. Think of the voices you've heard telling their own story of slavery: Equiano today, maybe others you've read or heard. If none come to mind, that's a starting place too. Hold this thought: real people wrote these accounts, and signed them with their own names. If you pray, you can pray for those whose stories were never written down. If you don't, just remember them. The bell holds the time.
Olaudah Equiano. A man kidnapped as a child and enslaved, who bought his freedom, became a Christian, and wrote and sold his own story to help end the slave trade.
Your line: tell the story. Today, read one page of an enslaved person's account, Equiano's or another, in that person's own words. Day nine hundred twelve.

913.title: Wilberforce (1807)
913.hook: a Christian member of Parliament campaigns year after year until Britain bans the slave trade
913.carry: you cannot say you did not know
913.howItsDone: Christians remember Wilberforce alongside Clarkson, Equiano and others in the campaign against the slave trade, and the Church of England keeps a commemoration of him in its calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Olaudah Equiano, who wrote his own story and put his name on the title page. Your line was tell the story. Whose own words did you read? Day nine hundred thirteen.

A vote is counted in the House of Commons, and the motion fails. The man who brought it goes home, and next session he brings it again. It fails again. Again he brings it. Again it fails. Year after year, a motion to end the British slave trade, and year after year it is voted down or stalled. Ships keep sailing. And he keeps standing up in that chamber with the same evidence in his hands. Today: Wilberforce.

William Wilberforce was a young member of Parliament, clever and well liked, when he went through an evangelical conversion. For a while he wondered whether a serious Christian should leave politics altogether. The usual account is that John Newton, the former slave-ship captain of Amazing Grace, urged him to stay where he was and use it. He stayed. He joined a campaign that was already moving: Quakers, the researcher Thomas Clarkson gathering evidence from sailors and ships, formerly enslaved writers like Equiano telling what they had lived. Wilberforce was its voice in Parliament. The campaign's great weapon was knowledge. A diagram of a slave ship, packed with bodies, was printed and passed around. Some ordinary people stopped buying slave-grown sugar. The argument was simple: now that you've seen it, you can't hide behind not knowing. A line often credited to Wilberforce, though its source is uncertain, puts it this way: you may look the other way, but you cannot say you did not know. The book of Proverbs had already asked: "If thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not; doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it?" And Paul's words fit the long fight: "let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not." In the end Parliament banned the trade. Not slavery itself, yet: that took another long campaign. But the ships were stopped by law. Some Christians had defended the trade, and some profited from it. Others, like Wilberforce, fought it from their faith. The story holds both.
screen: `A CONVERSION, AND A CHOICE TO STAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep going on a long good fight. Sit back, and let your hands rest. Name one good thing you're working for that is taking much longer than you hoped. A cause, a family repair, a habit, a hard conversation. Notice how many times you've wanted to drop it. Don't decide anything big. Just choose the next small step, the next bill you'll bring again. If you pray, you can ask for strength not to grow weary. If you don't, just hold the step. The bell holds the time.
Wilberforce. William Wilberforce, an evangelical member of Parliament who pressed the case against the British slave trade again and again until Parliament banned it.
Your line: you cannot say you did not know. Today, take the one small step you chose on your long good fight, even if nobody notices. Day nine hundred thirteen.

914.title: Sunday schools
914.hook: Robert Raikes starts schools on Sundays for children working in factories the rest of the week
914.howItsDone: Churches of different denominations hold Sunday school classes for children, and often for adults too, usually before or during the main service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wilberforce, bringing the same bill again and again. Your line was you cannot say you did not know. What small step did you take on your long good fight? Day nine hundred fourteen.
screen: `YOU CANNOT SAY YOU DID NOT KNOW.`

segments.voice: One day a week, the machines in an English factory town go quiet, and the children who work them are out in the streets: loud, ragged, bored, getting into fights, with no school to go to and no one to stop them. Neighbors complain. A newspaper man in Gloucester, Robert Raikes, looks at the same children and asks a different question. Not how do we keep them quiet, but what if they could read? Today's word is the answer he tried: Sunday schools.

Today Sunday school can mean a cheerful hour of Bible stories while the grown-ups are in church. It began as something tougher. Raikes's children worked during the week. Sunday was the only day they were free, so Sunday was the only day they could learn. He found women in the neighborhood who could teach, paid them, and opened classes in their homes. The children learned to read and to spell, and the book they read from was the Bible. They learned the catechism and went to church. They also, the accounts say, had to come with clean hands and combed hair. Raikes owned a newspaper, so he wrote about it, and the idea spread from town to town and across the sea. Tradition gives him the credit, though others had started Sunday classes before him. Behind it was a conviction that sounds obvious now and wasn't then: a poor child working in a factory was worth teaching. In Mark's Gospel, when the disciples try to shoo children away, Jesus is displeased and says: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." In King James English, suffer means let. Let them come. Not everyone liked it. Some people worried that teaching poor children to read would make them restless. Raikes kept the schools going anyway. To him, reading was a gift, not a danger.

Here's the practice: teach a child something. Rest your hands in your lap. Bring to mind a child you know: your own, a niece, a neighbor, a student, a kid at church. Or the child you used to be. What's one small thing you know that they don't yet? How to tie a knot. A word in another language. How to fold a paper boat. A line of a song or a psalm. Choose it. Think how you would show it, slowly, one step at a time. If you pray, you can pray for that child by name. If you don't, just wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Sunday schools. Classes started on the one free day of the week, so working children could learn to read, with the Bible as their book.
Your line: every child can learn. Today, teach that one small thing to a child, or to anyone younger than you, and let them take their time. Day nine hundred fourteen.

915.title: Block close: reforms
915.hook: Protestants and Catholics both reformed, both failed, both produced saints
915.howItsDone: Protestant and Catholic churches hold joint services and dialogues, and some have issued shared statements on the Reformation that admit wrongs on their own side.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sunday schools, reading lessons on the one free day for working children. Your line was every child can learn. What did you teach, and who learned it? Day nine hundred fifteen.

Lay out the faces from this block on a table, like old photographs. A monk with a list of theses for debate. A Dutchman turning back across the ice to pull his pursuer out. A soldier with a shattered leg reading saints' lives in bed. A nun on a dusty road founding small, poor convents. A man at the stake, praying for a king's eyes to be opened. A tinker writing in a jail cell. A preacher in a field. Some of them would not have shared a table with each other. Their churches put each other's people to death. And here they are, on one table, in one story. Today: the block close.

This block began with a church that needed reform, and with the line: always reforming. It ends with three honest sentences. Both reformed. Luther, Calvin, Menno Simons and Cranmer pressed for a church grounded in scripture, in the people's own language. Trent, Ignatius, Teresa and Francis de Sales renewed the Catholic Church from the inside: better trained priests, deeper prayer, gentler pastors. Both failed. Protestants executed Catholics and drowned Anabaptists. Catholics burned Protestants. Massacres in Paris, a war that tore Europe apart, kings using faith for power. Christians on each side did things this block could not soften. Both produced saints. Dirk Willems on the ice. Thomas More keeping his conscience. Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac feeding the poor. Wesley on horseback, starting the Methodist movement. Bunyan's Evangelist, writing about a burden that rolls away. And outside Europe, people like Las Casas, Kateri and Richard Allen carrying the same faith into very different lives. The book of Lamentations says: "Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD." The verse says our ways, not theirs. Some Reformed Christians use a phrase for this: a church reformed, and always being reformed. Catholics speak of the church always in need of purifying. And in John's Gospel, Jesus prays for his followers "That they all may be one". Some churches today tell this story together more than they used to, Protestants and Catholics admitting their own side's wounds. That is part of the reform too.

Here's the practice: pray for someone from the other side, or simply wish them well. Let your breath slow. Bring to mind one person on the other side of a divide from you. Another church, another faith, another politics, another side of a family quarrel. Hold the person, not their opinions. Then think of one thing on your own side that needs reform. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, and for yourself. If you don't, just wish them good. The bell holds the time.
Lamentations. The book whose line, let us search and try our ways, this block borrows to look honestly at its own reforms, failures, and saints.

Your line: reformed and reforming. Today, say one kind and true thing about a church or group you don't belong to. Tomorrow a new block begins: the modern church across the world. Day nine hundred fifteen.

916.title: William Carey
916.hook: a poor shoemaker who taught himself languages sails to India: expect great things, attempt great things
916.howItsDone: Baptists and other Protestants remember Carey as a pioneer of the modern missionary movement, and churches in India remember the translation work of Carey and his Indian colleagues.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the block close and its line from Lamentations: both reformed, both failed, both produced saints. Your line was reformed and reforming. What kind and true thing did you say about another church or group? Day nine hundred sixteen.

A new block begins today: the modern church across the world. It starts at a cobbler's bench in an English village. A young shoemaker sits mending boots, and propped up in front of him, the story goes, is a book in Latin or Greek, open while he works. On the wall hangs a homemade map of the world, with notes about the peoples of each land. He is poor. He has no university degree. He has taught himself to read languages his neighbors have never seen. And he has a question the older ministers would rather not hear. Today: William Carey.
screen: `A BOOK PROPPED ON THE COBBLER'S BENCH.`

segments.voice: His question was simple. Jesus told his disciples to go into all the world. Did that still apply to ordinary Christians, or was it only for the apostles? Carey, a Baptist preacher by now as well as a shoemaker, thought it still applied. A story is told that when he raised it at a meeting of ministers, an older man told him to sit down: if God wanted to reach the nations, God would do it without him. Carey didn't sit down for long. He wrote a pamphlet arguing his case, and then he preached a sermon on a verse from Isaiah: "Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes". Make the tent bigger. Out of that sermon, people remember a motto in two halves: expect great things from God, attempt great things for God. Notice the order. Expect comes first: the great things are looked for from God before they are attempted for God. Not long after, a missionary society was formed, and Carey sailed for India with his family. It was hard. Money ran short, there was illness and grief at home, and fruit came slowly. He worked, studied, and with colleagues set up a press and a college, and spent his life translating the Bible into languages of India, including Bengali. Indian scholars and Christians worked alongside him. And later readers have asked hard questions about how missions traveled with empire. That's tomorrow's story. Today's is a shoemaker who looked at a map and refused to make his tent smaller.

Here's the practice: attempt one big thing, starting small. Sit up, and let your feet rest flat on the floor. Picture your own tent: the size of your life right now. Is there one thing you've stopped hoping for because it seemed too big? A course, a reconciliation, a book, a move, a gift you'd love to give. Name it. Don't plan the whole thing. Just let yourself expect it for a minute. If you pray, you can bring it to God. If you don't, just hold it in your mind. The bell holds the time.
William Carey. An English shoemaker and Baptist preacher who taught himself languages, preached on enlarging the tent, sailed to India, and spent his life translating the Bible there.
Your line: expect great things. Today, take the very first step on that big thing: one call, one page, one form, one honest conversation. Day nine hundred sixteen.

917.title: Missions and empire, honestly
917.hook: missionaries brought schools and hospitals, and sometimes empire's arrogance; local Christians often led the growth
917.carry: the gospel is not an empire
917.howItsDone: Churches that began through missions, and churches that sent missionaries, sometimes look back on this history together, honoring local founders and naming the harm done alongside the good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, William Carey, the shoemaker who taught himself languages and sailed for India. Your line was expect great things. What big thing did you attempt? Day nine hundred seventeen.

A ship comes into harbor. On board, a missionary with a trunk of Bibles, and on the same ship, a soldier, a trader and a government clerk. They step onto the dock together. To the people watching from the shore, it can be hard to tell who works for whom. That picture sits at the center of a hard chapter in the Christian story. In the same years that European empires spread across Africa and Asia, missionaries went too. Some built schools and clinics and learned local languages with real love. Some carried the empire's pride with them. And in place after place, the faith grew through people whose names never made it home to Europe. Today, the honest version.

Start with what was good, because it was real. Missionaries opened schools, ran hospitals and clinics, and translated the Bible into languages that had never seen it in print. Some of them stood up to traders and officials on behalf of the people they lived among. Now the hard part, said plainly. Some missionaries treated local cultures as worthless, wanted converts to dress and sing and name their children like Europeans, and kept local Christians out of leadership for a long time. Some leaned on colonial power to get what they wanted. Some Christians today, in the churches those missions founded and in the churches that sent them, say this openly. Then there's the part that's easy to miss. The faith often spread through local people: catechists, evangelists, Bible women, translators. In West Africa a Liberian preacher, William Wadé Harris, walked the coast in a white robe with a cross and a Bible, and tradition says crowds were baptized after hearing him. In India, Pandita Ramabai, a scholar of Sanskrit, became a Christian and opened homes for widows and girls. These were not stand-ins for foreigners. They led. Underneath it all is a line Jesus spoke, in the King James Bible: "Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them. But it shall not be so among you." And before Pilate, he said: "My kingdom is not of this world." Some Christians who look back on this history return to those words. The gospel, they say, came with an empire. It was never meant to be one. Look back over this whole week: Richard Allen walking out, Equiano telling his story, Wilberforce, Sunday schools, Carey. Again and again, change came from people at the edges, and from those who listened to them.
screen: `IT SHALL NOT BE SO AMONG YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one local church leader's name. Not a famous visitor. Someone from the place itself. Today it could be Harris, or Ramabai, or a pastor in your own town whose name you've never asked. Settle first, and breathe. Bring to mind the people who are usually left out of the story: the translator, the evangelist who walked, the woman who taught the first class. Hold one of them for a moment. Say the name quietly. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If you don't, let the name sit beside the famous ones, just as large. The bell holds the time.
Ramabai. A Sanskrit scholar in India who became a Christian and opened homes for widows and girls, leading her own mission rather than following a foreign one.
Your line: the gospel is not an empire. Today, when you help someone, notice whether you're also trying to make them more like you. Day nine hundred seventeen.

original.note: Greek: kingdom or reign, the word in John 18:36, my kingdom is not of this world.

trapdoor: what you thought: missionaries were either heroes or villains.
what it means: they brought schools and hospitals, and sometimes the empire's pride; local Christians often led the growth.
what a scholar hears: Jesus's own line that the rulers of the nations lord it over people, "but it shall not be so among you," read as a judgment on the church's alliance with power.

sources.ref: Lives of William Wadé Harris and Pandita Ramabai (standard biographies)
